# Introduction to Deep Sleep  {.unnumbered}

The ESP32 is a powerful microcontroller, but it is not frugal. With the CPU running and the radio off, it draws around 20–70 mA depending on the CPU frequency (ESP32 datasheet), and over 100 mA when Wi-Fi is active. Constantly awake, it would drain a typical 2000 mAh battery in one or two days.

To build a station that can run for months on a battery, we use **Deep Sleep**.

## What is Deep Sleep?

> **Further Reading:** For a comprehensive overview of the ESP32 deep sleep states, you can refer to this [uPesy tutorial on Deep Sleep](https://www.upesy.fr/blogs/tutorials/how-to-use-deep-sleep-on-esp32-to-reduce-power-consumption).

Deep sleep puts the ESP32 into a state where almost everything shuts down:

*   The two main CPU cores are powered off. Only the **RTC subsystem** stays on: a low-power timer, the RTC memory, the wake-up logic, and optionally the **ULP (Ultra Low Power) coprocessor**, a tiny processor that can run simple programs if you write one for it (we won't).
*   Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios are completely disabled.
*   The Flash and the main system memory (RAM) are no longer powered. Only the special **RTC memory** remains active and usable.

In this state, the ESP32 **chip** draws around **10 µA** (datasheet value, RTC timer and RTC memory on), up to about 150 µA if the ULP coprocessor is running.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Chip vs. board consumption
These figures are for the ESP32 chip alone. A development board adds its own consumers: the voltage regulator, the USB-to-serial chip, the power LED. Each module on the breadboard also adds its own (see [Hardware Modifications](02-hardware-modifications.qmd)). The real consumption of the whole station in deep sleep is therefore higher, often by an order of magnitude on a standard DevKit.
:::

### RAM Erasure and RTC_DATA_ATTR

Because the main CPU and RAM are unpowered during deep sleep, all standard variables saved in RAM are completely erased. 

Fortunately, the RTC RAM remains powered. If we need to keep track of data across deep sleep cycles (for example, storing a boot counter to track how many times the ESP32 has woken up), we can force the ESP32 to save the variable in this special memory by adding the `RTC_DATA_ATTR` attribute to its declaration.

### The Deep Sleep Paradigm (`setup` vs `loop`)

In Phase 01, our code relied on the standard Arduino structure: we initialized our sensors in the `setup()` function once, and then continuously took measurements and called `delay()` inside the `loop()` function.

Deep sleep changes this. When the ESP32 wakes up from deep sleep, it restarts from scratch: `setup()` runs from the beginning, and once it reaches the command to go back to sleep, execution stops. In a deep sleep application, `loop()` is therefore **never called**.

## Wake-up Sources

After putting the ESP32 into deep sleep, there are several ways to wake it back up. We must configure a **Wake-up Source** before telling the ESP32 to go to sleep:

### 1. Internal Timer Wake-up
The ESP32 has an internal timer in its RTC subsystem. You can tell it to sleep for a specific number of microseconds, and it will automatically wake itself up when the time expires.

Here is a quick "Hello Deep Sleep" example using the internal timer:

```cpp
#include <Arduino.h>

// Conversion factor for micro seconds to seconds
#define uS_TO_S_FACTOR 1000000ULL  
#define TIME_TO_SLEEP  10          // Sleep for 10 seconds

void setup(){
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(1000); 
  
  Serial.println("Waking up! Reading sensors...");
  // ... (Your sensor code would go here) ...
  
  Serial.println("Going to sleep for 10 seconds.");
  Serial.flush(); 
  
  // Configure the timer wake-up
  esp_sleep_enable_timer_wakeup(TIME_TO_SLEEP * uS_TO_S_FACTOR);
  
  // Enter deep sleep
  esp_deep_sleep_start();
}

void loop(){
  // This is never reached because esp_deep_sleep_start() halts execution!
}
```

> **Ready-to-use project:** The complete code for this deep sleep example is available in the repository here: [`04_deep_sleep_timer`](https://github.com/wg1d/personal-autonomous-weather-station/tree/main/firmware/PoC/Phase-02/04_deep_sleep_timer)

*   **Pros:** Requires no external hardware or wiring. Extremely easy to program in software as seen above.
*   **Cons:** By default, the timer runs on the internal 150 kHz RC oscillator, which is not temperature-compensated and can drift by several percent. With a 15-minute interval, a 5 % error means waking up about 45 seconds early or late, every cycle. The wake-ups also say nothing about the absolute time: we would still need the external RTC for timestamps.

### 2. Capacitive Touch Pins
The ESP32 has several pins that act as capacitive touch sensors. You can configure the ESP32 to wake up simply when a user physically touches one of these pins.

### 3. RTC Pins (External Interrupt EXT0 / EXT1)
You can configure the ESP32 to wake up when an electrical signal on a specific RTC pin changes state (e.g., goes from 3.3V down to 0V). This is useful to wake up the ESP32 immediately when a user presses a physical button, when a magnetic hall sensor detects a door opening, or when a PIR motion sensor detects movement.

*   **Pros:** Allows an external component to dictate the schedule.
*   **Cons:** Requires additional hardware (like an external RTC module or sensor) and extra wiring. Only RTC-capable GPIOs can be used (see the pinout).

## Why We Use the DS3231 RTC Alarms

Because weather data relies on accurate timestamps, and because an outdoor station is exposed to large temperature variations, we do not rely on the ESP32's internal timer.

Instead, we use the **DS3231 RTC** installed in Phase 01. The DS3231 contains a Temperature Compensated Crystal Oscillator (TCXO): its datasheet specifies ±2 ppm from 0 °C to 40 °C (about one minute per year), and ±3.5 ppm over the full industrial range. The same chip gives us both the wake-up schedule and the timestamps.

We will program a hardware **Alarm** inside the DS3231. When the alarm triggers, the DS3231 will pull its **SQW (Square Wave)** pin LOW. By wiring this SQW pin to the ESP32 and configuring an `EXT0` external wake-up, the DS3231 wakes the ESP32 up exactly when a reading is required.

In the next chapter, we modify the circuit to connect this wake-up pin, and we add a way to cut the power of the SD card module during sleep.
